4. Diagnosis and assessment of paƟents with hypertension

  4.1 Diagnosis

The diagnosis of hypertension should be based on mulƟple blood pressure measurements,
taken on separate occasions over a period. BP can be highly variable; thus, the diagnosis of
hypertension should not be based on a single set of BP readings at a single oﬃce visit. In
general, the diagnosis of hypertension should be based on at least three blood pressure
measurements per visit and at least two to three visits at 1–4-week intervals (depending on
the BP level) to conﬁrm the diagnosis of hypertension9.


The diagnosis might be made on a single  visit,  if BP  is ≥160/100 mmHg or there  is
accompanying evidence of hypertension mediated organ damage (HMOD) (e.g., hypertensive
reƟnopathy with exudates and hemorrhages, or LVH, or vascular or renal damage)10. When
the iniƟal SBP is between 140 and 159 mmHg, or the DBP is between 90 and 99 mmHg, repeat
measurements should be performed on three separate occasions within a period of 1 to 4
weeks to determine whether a diagnosis of hypertension is valid. All measurements should
be taken in the same arm.  If possible and available, the diagnosis of hypertension should be
conﬁrmed by out-of-oﬃce BP measurement (i.e., HBPM and/or ABPM)9.


In the iniƟal evaluaƟon, measurement of blood pressure should be performed in both arms.
If the diﬀerence in readings between arms is more than 10 mmHg, repeat the measurements
at 1-2 mins interval. If the diﬀerence in readings between arms remains more than 10 mmHg
on the second measurement, measure subsequent blood pressures in the arm with the higher
reading and it should be noted. If the diﬀerence is >20 mmHg, consider further invesƟgaƟon9.

If hypertension is not diagnosed, measure the person's clinic blood pressure at least every 3
years subsequently, and consider measuring it more frequently if the person's clinic blood
pressure is close to 140/90 mmHg (Table 3).

  4.2 Clinical evaluaƟon and assessment of hypertension
4.2.1 Clinical evaluaƟon:

The goals of the iniƟal evaluaƟon of the hypertensive paƟent are to
   1. Establish the diagnosis and grade of hypertension.
   2. Screening for potenƟal secondary causes of hypertension.
   3. IdenƟfy factors that potenƟally contribute to development of hypertension (lifestyle,
     concomitant medicaƟons, or family history).
   4. IdenƟfy concomitant CV risk factors (including lifestyle and family history) (Table 4)
   5. IdenƟfy concomitant diseases and establish whether there is evidence of HMOD or
     exisƟng cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, or renal disease. (Table 5)

These goals are usually accomplished by a thorough medical history, physical examinaƟon,
and simple laboratory invesƟgaƟons. While waiƟng for conﬁrmaƟon of a diagnosis of
hypertension, carry out some rouƟne invesƟgaƟons for assessment of HMOD. If
hypertension is not diagnosed but there is evidence of HMOD, consider carrying out
invesƟgaƟons for alternaƟve causes of HMOD.

History

Most paƟents with hypertension are asymptomaƟc, the high blood pressure usually having
been noted during an incidental clinical examinaƟon. A proporƟon of paƟents will present
with a major complicaƟon of hypertension such as stroke or myocardial infarcƟon, but only a
small number will present with symptoms directly aƩributable to hypertension such as
breathlessness or headache. That is why hypertension is called a ‘Silent killer’. The key issues
that need to be addressed in the history include:
Risk factors assessment:
    *  Family and personal history of hypertension, CVD, stroke, or renal disease.
    *  Family  and  personal   history   of   associated   risk   factors   (e.g.,   familial
       hypercholesterolaemia)
    *   Dietary history and salt intake
    *  Smoking history
    *  Alcohol consumpƟon
    *   History of physical exercise/sedentary lifestyle
    *   History of erecƟle dysfuncƟon

4.2.2 InvesƟgaƟons

All hypertensive paƟents should undergo a limited number of invesƟgaƟons. However, when
starƟng pharmacological therapy for hypertension, WHO suggests obtaining tests to screen
for comorbidiƟes and secondary hypertension, but only when tesƟng does not delay or
impede starƟng treatment. In low-resourced areas or non-clinical seƫngs, where tesƟng may
not be possible because of addiƟonal costs, and lack of access to laboratories and ECG,
treatment should not be delayed, and tesƟng can be done subsequently. Some medicines,
such as long-acƟng dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers (CCBs) are more   suitable for
iniƟaƟon without tesƟng, compared to diureƟcs or angiotensin-converƟng enzyme inhibitors
(ACEi)/angiotensin-II receptor blockers (ARBs)12.
All hypertensive paƟents should undergo a limited number of invesƟgaƟons, these include: -

                rate, (eGFR)

    Urine analysis: DipsƟck urine test
    12-lead ECG for detecƟon of atrial ﬁbrillaƟon, leŌ ventricular hypertrophy (LVH),
       ischemic heart disease.

For most paƟents: -
   Haemoglobin and/or haematocrit
    Chest X-ray: to detect cardiomegaly, heart failure, coarctaƟon of the aorta
    Echocardiogram: to detect or quanƟfy leŌ ventricular hypertrophy
The nature and scale of further invesƟgaƟons will be determined by the index of suspicion
of a secondary cause for hypertension and assessment for HMOD

5.3.5 Goals for BP lowering treatment

Eﬀorts must be made to reach the target BP level. These targets should be reached within 3
months. In general, once the BP is controlled, most paƟents will require life-long treatment.
   A target blood pressure treatment goal of <140/90 mmHg in all paƟents with
      hypertension without comorbidiƟes.
 A target systolic blood pressure treatment goal of <130 mmHg in high-risk paƟents
      with hypertension (those with high CVD risk, known CVD, diabetes mellitus,
       chronic kidney disease)10.

5.3.6 When to Refer

  PaƟents with the following condiƟons should be referred to the appropriate specialist for
  further assessment. IndicaƟons for referral to the appropriate specialist include:
        accelerated or malignant hypertension
       suspected secondary hypertension
        resistant hypertension
        recent onset of target organ damage
       pregnancy
        children <18 years old
